fetched_contents.text: Part 10.4: Hypothermia Unintentional hypothermia is a serious and preventable health problem. Severe hypothermia (body temperature <30°C [86°F]) is associated with marked depression of critical body functions that may make the victim appear clinically dead during the initial assessment. But in some cases hypothermia may exert a protective effect on the brain and organs in cardiac arrest.1,2 Intact neurologic recovery may be possible after hypothermic cardiac arrest, although those with nonasphyxial arrest have a better prognosis than those with asphyxial-associated hypothermic arrest.3–5 With this in mind, lifesaving procedures should not be withheld on the basis of clinical presentation.4 Victims should be transported as soon as possible to a center where monitored rewarming is possible. General Care for All Victims of Hypothermia When the victim is extremely cold but has maintained a perfusing rhythm, the rescuer should focus on interventions that prevent further heat loss and begin to rewarm the victim. These include the following: • Prevent additional evaporative heat loss by removing wet garments and insulating the victim from further environmental exposures. • Do not delay urgent procedures, such as intubation and insertion of vascular catheters, but perform them gently while closely monitoring cardiac rhythm. These patients are prone to develop ventricular fibrillation (VF). For patients with moderate to severe hypothermia, therapy is determined by the presence or absence of a perfusing rhythm. We provide an overview of therapy here and give more details below. Management of the patient with moderate to severe hypothermia is as follows: • Hypothermia with a perfusing rhythm –Mild (>34°C [>93.2°F]): passive rewarming –Moderate (30°C to 34°C [86°F to 93.2°F]): active external rewarming –Severe (<30°C [86°F]): active internal rewarming; consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation • Patients in cardiac arrest will require CPR with some modifications of conventional BLS and ACLS care and will require active internal rewarming –Moderate (30°C to 34°C [86°F to 93.2°F]): start CPR, attempt defibrillation, establish IV access, give IV medications spaced at longer intervals, provide active internal rewarming –Severe (<30°C [86°F]): start CPR, attempt defibrillation once, withhold medications until temperature >30°C (86°F), provide active internal rewarming –Patients with a core temperature of >34°C (>93.2°F) may be passively rewarmed with warmed blankets and a warm environment. This form of rewarming will not be adequate for a patient with cardiopulmonary arrest or severe hypothermia.6 –For patients with moderate hypothermia (30°C to 34°C [86°F to 93.2°F]) and a perfusing rhythm and no preceding cardiac arrest, active external warming (with heating blankets, forced air, and warmed infusion) should be considered (Class IIb). Active external rewarming uses heating methods or devices (radiant heat, forced hot air, warmed IV fluids, warm water packs) but no invasive devices. Use of these methods requires careful monitoring for hemodynamic changes and tissue injury from external heating devices. Some researchers believe that active external rewarming contributes to “afterdrop” (continued drop in core temperature when cold blood from the periphery is mobilized). But recent studies have indicated that forced air rewarming (one study used warmed IV fluids and forced air rewarming) is effective in some patients, even those with severe hypothermia.7,8 –For patients with a core body temperature <30°C (86°F) and cardiac arrest, active internal rewarming techniques (invasive) are needed. With or without return of spontaneous circulation, these patients may benefit from prolonged CPR and internal warming (peritoneal lavage, esophageal rewarming tubes, cardiopulmonary bypass, extracorporeal circulation, etc). Modifications of BLS for Hypothermia If the hypothermic victim has not yet developed cardiac arrest, focus attention on warming the patient with available methods. Handle the victim gently for all procedures; physical manipulations have been reported to precipitate VF.4,9 If the hypothermic victim is in cardiac arrest, the general approach to BLS management should still target airway, breathing, and circulation but with some modifications in approach. When the victim is hypothermic, pulse and respiratory rates may be slow or difficult to detect. For these reasons the BLS healthcare provider should assess breathing and later assess the pulse for a period of 30 to 45 seconds to confirm respiratory arrest, pulseless cardiac arrest, or bradycardia that is profound enough to require CPR.10 If the victim is not breathing, start rescue breathing immediately. If possible, administer warmed (42°C to 46°C [108°F to 115°F]) humidified oxygen during bag-mask ventilation. If the victim is pulseless with no detectable signs of circulation, start chest compressions immediately. If there is any doubt about whether a pulse is present, begin compressions. The temperature at which defibrillation should first be attempted in the severely hypothermic patient and the number of defibrillation attempts that should be made have not been established. But if ventricular tachycardia (VT) or VF is present, defibrillation should be attempted. Automated external defibrillators (AEDs) may be used for these patients. If VF is detected, it should be treated with 1 shock then immediately followed by resumption of CPR, as outlined elsewhere in these guidelines for VF/VT (see Part 5: “Electrical Therapies: Automated External Defibrillators, Defibrillation, Cardioversion, and Pacing”). If the patient does not respond to 1 shock, further defibrillation attempts should be deferred, and the rescuer should focus on continuing CPR and rewarming the patient to a range of 30°C to 32°C (86°F to 89.6°F) before repeating the defibrillation attempt. fetched_contents.text: Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update Abstract Accidental hypothermia is an unintentional drop of core temperature below 35 °C. Annually, thousands die of primary hypothermia and an unknown number die of secondary hypothermia worldwide. Hypothermia can be expected in emergency patients in the prehospital phase. Injured and intoxicated patients cool quickly even in subtropical regions. Preventive measures are important to avoid hypothermia or cooling in ill or injured patients. Diagnosis and assessment of the risk of cardiac arrest are based on clinical signs and core temperature measurement when available. Hypothermic patients with risk factors for imminent cardiac arrest (temperature < 30 °C in young and healthy patients and <32 °C in elderly persons, or patients with multiple comorbidities), ventricular dysrhythmias, or systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg) and hypothermic patients who are already in cardiac arrest, should be transferred directly to an extracorporeal life support (ECLS) centre. If a hypothermic patient arrests, continuous cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be performed. In hypothermic patients, the chances of survival and good neurological outcome are higher than for normothermic patients for witnessed, unwitnessed and asystolic cardiac arrest. Mechanical CPR devices should be used for prolonged rescue, if available. In severely hypothermic patients in cardiac arrest, if continuous or mechanical CPR is not possible, intermittent CPR should be used. Rewarming can be accomplished by passive and active techniques. Most often, passive and active external techniques are used. Only in patients with refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest are internal rewarming techniques required. ECLS rewarming should be performed with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). A post-resuscitation care bundle should complement treatment. Keywords: accidental hypothermia, cardiac arrest, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, emergency medicine, extracorporeal life support, rewarming 1. Introduction Accidental hypothermia is the involuntary drop of the core temperature below 35 °C [1]. Accidental hypothermia may be caused in a healthy subject by exposure to a cold environment (primary accidental hypothermia) or triggered by other conditions, most commonly illness, intoxication, or trauma, called secondary hypothermia (Table 1). The pathophysiology of accidental hypothermia in injured or ill patients has been described in detail elsewhere [2]. This article does not cover therapeutic hypothermia, which is intentionally-induced hypothermia used in fields such as cardiac surgery, and as part of a post-resuscitation care bundle after cardiac arrest in neonates and adults. Hypothermia has detrimental effects on the function of multiple organs, including heart, brain, kidney, blood coagulation, and, possibly, the immune system [4,5]. Overall, accidental hypothermia increases morbidity and mortality in affected victims. The aim of this work is to provide an up-to-date overview on clinical aspects of accidental hypothermia. 2. Epidemiology Accidental hypothermia has been recognised since ancient times [6]. Throughout history, hypothermia has been a disease of war and disasters such as avalanches, earthquakes and tsunamis [7,8,9]. Nowadays in developed countries, primary hypothermia affects mainly people who live, work, and recreate outdoors putting themselves at risk in cold environments and homeless people. In less developed countries primary hypothermia affects homeless people and people in mass accidents; for example, victims of avalanches burying villages and travellers in poorly protected mountain areas. In general, the risk of accidental hypothermia from exposure to cold increases with decreasing temperature, but many cases among homeless individuals occur during periods of low and moderate cold stress [10]. Secondary hypothermia has been recognised as a phenomenon in elderly and patients with multiple comorbidities, mainly in Japan, which has the oldest population worldwide [11]. Countries with comparably old populations may see similar rises in coming decades. In the United States, primary hypothermia is the cause of at least 1500 deaths a year. From 1995 to 2004 about 15,000 patients presented annually to hospitals with hypothermia and other cold-related conditions [12]. The incidence of accidental hypothermia in European countries and New Zealand ranges from 0.13 to 6.9 cases per 100,000 per year [13,14,15,16]. Hypothermia is responsible for about 2 deaths per 100,000 per year in Scotland and 5 per 100,000 per year in Poland [17,18]. Frequencies vary widely because for most countries no reliable national data are available. fetched_contents.text: Accidental hypothermia in adults: Clinical manifestations and evaluation INTRODUCTION — Death from exposure and accidental hypothermia occurs throughout the world and can present significant management problems [1-4]. While typically associated with regions of the world with severe winters, hypothermia is also seen in areas with milder climates, such as the southern United States [5,6]. Hypothermia can occur during the summer months and in hospitalized patients [7]. The definition, pathophysiology, and evaluation of accidental hypothermia will be discussed here. A table and algorithm outlining the emergency management of hypothermia in adults are provided (table 1 and algorithm 1). A temperature unit conversion calculator is provided (calculator 1). The following related content is discussed separately: ●Management of accidental hypothermia in adults (see "Accidental hypothermia in adults: Management") ●Drowning, often complicated by hypothermia (see "Drowning (submersion injuries)") ●External injuries from cold (see "Frostbite: Acute care and prevention" and "Nonfreezing cold water (trench foot) and warm water immersion injuries") ●Accidental hypothermia in children (see "Hypothermia in children: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis" and "Hypothermia in children: Management") DEFINITIONS AND STAGES OF HYPOTHERMIA Commonly used definition and stages — Hypothermia is defined as a core temperature below 35°C (95°F). The stage of hypothermia, defined by core temperature, has a large impact on both recognition and treatment. The most commonly used definitions found in the literature are as follows [8,9]: ●Mild hypothermia – Core temperature 32 to 35°C (90 to 95°F) ●Moderate hypothermia – Core temperature 28 to 32°C (82 to 90°F) ●Severe hypothermia – Core temperature <28°C (82°F) In addition, some experts regard a core temperature <24°C (75°F) or <20°C (68°F) as "profound hypothermia" [10,11]. Because the clinical features of hypothermia differ among patients, and because core temperature measurement is imprecise, the recognition of each stage is more important than exact temperature cut-offs. Prehospital personnel should measure core temperature, preferably using an esophageal probe in the lower third of the esophagus, in an unresponsive patient who is tracheally intubated. (See 'Temperature measurement' below.) If temperature measurement is not feasible, prehospital personnel should estimate the severity of hypothermia by observing clinical signs. Because the response to hypothermia varies widely among patients, any clinical staging system can only provide a rough estimate of severity (table 2) [12]. ●Cold stress (not hypothermia) – Normal mental status with shivering. Functioning normally. Able to care for self. Estimated core temperature 35 to 37°C (95 to 98.6°F). ●Mild hypothermia – Alert, but mental status may be altered. Shivering present. Not functioning normally. Not able to care for self. Estimated core temperature 32 to 35°C (90 to 95°F). ●Moderate hypothermia – Decreased level of consciousness. Conscious or unconscious, with or without shivering. Estimated core temperature 28 to 32°C (82 to 90°F). ●Severe/profound hypothermia – Unconscious. Not shivering. Estimated core temperature <28°C (<82°F). Other staging systems — Prehospital personnel, especially in Europe, may use the clinical staging scale described by the International Commission for Mountain Emergency Medicine, sometimes referred to as "the Swiss system" (table 3) [10]: ●Mild (HT I) – Normal mental status with shivering. Estimated core temperature 32 to 35°C (90 to 95°F). ●Moderate (HT II) – Altered mental status without shivering. Estimated core temperature 28 to 32°C (82 to 90°F). ●Severe (HT III) – Unconscious. Estimated core temperature 24 to 28°C (75 to 82°F). ●Severe (HT IV) – Apparent death. Core temperature 13.7 to 24°C (56.7 to 75°F) (resuscitation may be possible). ●Death (HT V) – Death due to irreversible hypothermia. Core temperature <9 to 13.7°C (<48.2 to 56.7°F) (resuscitation not possible). A limitation of the Swiss staging system is that shivering may not cease until around 30°C (86°F). In addition, vital signs and other signs of life may be present at core temperatures below 24°C (75°F) [13,14]. An analysis of published case reports found a high degree of overlap of core temperatures among the stages and many cases in which the Swiss system overestimated core temperature [15]. The lowest observed core temperatures were 28.1°C (82.6°F) for HT 1, 22.1°C (71.8°F) for HT II, and 19.3°C (66.7°F) for HT III. A further analysis of 305 hospital and published cases found that only 61 percent of patients were assigned to the correct stage [16]. There were large overlaps among the four stages. Core temperature was overestimated in 18 percent and underestimated in 21 percent of patients. The authors calculated that the optimal temperature thresholds to classify patients into the four stages were 32.1, 27.5, and 24°C (89.8, 81.5, and 75°F), which are similar to the original cutoffs of 32, 28, and 24°C (90, 82, and 75°F). The Swiss system is being replaced by the Revised Swiss System (RSS) as a recommendation of the International Commission for Mountain Emergency Medicine [17]. The RSS stages hypothermia based on the level of consciousness (using the Alert, Verbal, Painful, Unconscious [AVPU] scale) and the presence or absence of vital signs (figure 1). Shivering is no longer a stage-defining sign. The emphasis of the RSS is on the risk of cardiac arrest rather than core temperature. Alert patients (mild hypothermia) have a low risk of cardiac arrest, patients who respond to verbal stimuli have a moderate risk, and patients who respond only to painful stimuli or have no response (unconscious) have a high risk. Patients who are unconscious without detectable vital signs are considered to be in hypothermic cardiac arrest. Algorithmic decision points for active external vs active internal rewarming

The evidence supports a staged algorithm rather than a single blunt cutoff: external rewarming is usually the first choice for moderate hypothermia, whereas active internal rewarming becomes more urgent when the patient is in cardiac arrest, has severe hypothermia, or is refractory to external rewarming. The clearest decision point is core temperature: moderate hypothermia is defined as core temperature 30°C to 34°C, and severe hypothermia as <30°C [N1-F1]. That is also the practical threshold for choosing external vs internal rewarming.

Key clinical signs that favor external rewarming over internal rewarming
External rewarming is preferred when the patient has a perfusing rhythm, no cardiac arrest, and moderate hypothermia. The guideline explicitly states that for patients with a perfusing rhythm and moderate hypothermia, active external rewarming is appropriate [N1-F1]. It also says that most often passive and active external techniques are used, and internal rewarming is reserved only for refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest [N1-R2]. The 2021 NIH update similarly says that passive and active external techniques are most often used, and internal rewarming is required only in refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest [N5-F2]. So external rewarming is favored when:
- the patient is alert or has a perfusing rhythm,
- the temperature is in the moderate range (30°C–34°C),
- rewarming can be done safely with external methods such as blankets, forced air, warmed IV fluids, or warm water packs [N1-F1][N2-R2][N4-R1].

Key clinical signs that favor internal rewarming over external rewarming
Internal rewarming is preferred when the patient is in cardiac arrest, has severe hypothermia, or is refractory to external rewarming. The 2005 Circulation guideline states that for patients with a core body temperature <30°C and cardiac arrest, active internal rewarming techniques are needed [N1-R1]. It also says that severe hypothermia (<30°C) may require active internal rewarming; consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [N1-F1]. The NIH update similarly says that if a hypothermic patient arrests, continuous CPR should be performed and internal rewarming should be considered, especially if continuous or mechanical CPR is not possible [N5-F2]. So internal rewarming is favored when:
- the patient is in cardiac arrest,
- the temperature is <30°C,
- the patient is refractory to external rewarming,
- or extracorporeal rewarming such as ECMO is indicated [N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-F2].

When to escalate rewarming intensity or consider combined approaches
Escalation is indicated when external rewarming is insufficient or the patient remains hemodynamically unstable. The Circulation guideline notes that active external rewarming uses heating methods or devices but requires careful monitoring for hemodynamic changes and tissue injury from external heating devices [N1-F1]. It also says that severe hypothermia may require active internal rewarming; consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [N1-F1]. The 2021 NIH update similarly says that only in patients with refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest are internal rewarming techniques required [N5-F2]. So escalation or combined approaches are appropriate when:
- rewarming is not producing sufficient core temperature increase,
- the patient remains hemodynamically unstable,
- or the patient is refractory to external rewarming [N1-F1][N5-F2].

The evidence is thin on a precise “rapid decision matrix,” but the strongest algorithmic logic is temperature plus rhythm: moderate hypothermia with a perfusing rhythm → external rewarming; severe hypothermia or cardiac arrest → internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming [N1-F1][N5-F2].
node_outputs.N10:
Practical management steps and monitoring during active rewarming

Initial stabilization steps before rewarming
Before starting rewarming, the patient should be stabilized to prevent further heat loss and to ensure that urgent procedures can be performed safely. The Circulation guideline says that for patients who are extremely cold but have maintained a perfusing rhythm, the rescuer should focus on interventions that prevent further heat loss and begin rewarming [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes removing wet garments, insulating the patient from further environmental exposures, and performing urgent procedures such as intubation and vascular catheterization gently while closely monitoring cardiac rhythm [N1-F1]. The NIH update similarly says that rewarming can be accomplished by passive and active techniques, and most often passive and active external techniques are used, while only internal rewarming is required in refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest [N5-F2]. So initial stabilization includes:
- removing wet clothing,
- protecting the patient from further heat loss,
- intubation and vascular access when needed,
- gentle handling to avoid arrhythmias [N1-F1][N5-F2].

Monitoring parameters during rewarming
Monitoring during rewarming should be comprehensive and continuous. The Circulation guideline specifically mentions monitoring for hemodynamic changes and tissue injury from external heating devices [N1-F1]. It also notes that in moderate to severe hypothermia, therapy is determined by the presence or absence of a perfusing rhythm and that patients are prone to develop ventricular fibrillation [N1-F1]. The NIH update similarly emphasizes that rewarming should be performed with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation if needed, and that the patient should be monitored closely [N5-F2]. The EMCrit Project adds that hypothermia itself causes bradycardia and that trying to speed up the heart with medications or pacing is generally a mistake, as it may precipitate arrhythmias [N4-R3]. So key monitoring parameters during rewarming include:
- core temperature,
- ECG,
- hemodynamic parameters (blood pressure, heart rate, rhythm),
- signs of arrhythmia,
- evidence of tissue injury from external rewarming,
- rewarming rate and response [N1-F1][N4-R3][N5-F2].

When to switch rewarming modality or pause rewarming
Rewarming should be switched or paused when the patient becomes unstable or when external rewarming is not sufficient. The Circulation guideline says that active external rewarming requires careful monitoring for hemodynamic changes and tissue injury and that severe hypothermia may require active internal rewarming; consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [N1-F1]. It also says that if the patient is in cardiac arrest, active internal rewarming is needed [N1-R1]. The NIH update similarly says that only in patients with refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest are internal rewarming techniques required [N5-F2]. The 2020 Wilderness Medical Society CPG says that if the body temperature is below 30°C, only one attempt should be made, and further attempts are indicated once the temperature is greater than 30°C [N7-R3]. So the guidance is:
- switch to internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming if the patient is refractory to external rewarming or in cardiac arrest,
- pause rewarming if hemodynamic instability develops,
- consider temporary reduction or pause if rewarming is causing tissue injury or arrhythmias,
- follow the 30°C threshold for deciding whether to continue external rewarming [N1-F1][N5-F2][N7-R3].
node_outputs.N8:
Guideline-based framework for hypothermia severity and rewarming strategy

Core temperature thresholds for classification and intervention
The evidence supports a clear temperature-based classification system. The 2021 NIH update defines accidental hypothermia as a core temperature below 35°C, and divides hypothermia into stages based on core temperature [N5-F2]. The Circulation guideline similarly defines mild hypothermia as core temperature >34°C, moderate hypothermia as 30°C–34°C, and severe hypothermia as <30°C [N1-F1]. The UpToDate section on accidental hypothermia in adults adds that moderate hypothermia is core temperature 28°C–32°C, severe hypothermia is <28°C, and profound hypothermia may be <24°C or <20°C [N6-F3]. So the most defensible thresholds in the evidence are:
- mild hypothermia: >34°C,
- moderate hypothermia: 30°C–34°C,
- severe hypothermia: <30°C,
- profound hypothermia: <24°C or <20°C [N1-F1][N5-F2][N6-F3].

When to initiate rewarming and which rewarming mode is preferred
Rewarming should be initiated early, especially when the patient is at risk of cardiac arrest or has a low core temperature. The Circulation guideline says rewarming should start prehospital, and for patients with a perfusing rhythm and moderate hypothermia, active external rewarming is appropriate [N1-F1]. It also says that severe hypothermia may require active internal rewarming; consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [N1-F1]. The NIH update similarly says that rewarming can be accomplished by passive and active techniques, and most often passive and active external techniques are used, while only internal rewarming is required in refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest [N5-F2]. The 2021 NIH update also says that hypothermic patients with risk factors for imminent cardiac arrest should be transferred directly to an ECLS center, and continuous CPR should be performed if the patient arrests [N5-F2]. So the preferred strategy is:
- start rewarming prehospital if possible,
- use passive and active external rewarming for moderate hypothermia,
- use active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming for severe hypothermia or cardiac arrest,
- consider ECLS if the patient is refractory or in cardiac arrest [N1-F1][N5-F2].

Contraindications or exceptions to active rewarming
Active rewarming is not contraindicated in most hypothermic patients, but it is not the first choice when the patient is in cardiac arrest or when external rewarming is refractory. The NIH update says that only in patients with refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest are internal rewarming techniques required [N5-F2]. The Circulation guideline similarly says that severe hypothermia may require active internal rewarming; consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [N1-F1]. The 2020 Wilderness Medical Society CPG adds that if the body temperature is below 30°C, only one attempt should be made, and further attempts are indicated once the temperature is greater than 30°C [N7-R3]. So the exceptions are:
- cardiac arrest: active internal rewarming is needed rather than continuing only external rewarming,
- refractory hypothermia: internal rewarming is required,
- temperatures below 30°C may require one cautious attempt only before deciding on further rewarming intensity [N1-F1][N5-F2][N7-R3].

Overall, the evidence supports a temperature-guided, rhythm-guided, and risk-guided framework: moderate hypothermia → external rewarming; severe hypothermia or cardiac arrest → internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming [N1-F1][N5-F2].
node_outputs.N11:
Evidence-based considerations for urgent patient with 28°C and severe bradycardia

Urgency of rewarming in 28°C hypothermia
The evidence clearly indicates urgency when the core temperature is 28°C. The Circulation guideline defines severe hypothermia as core temperature <30°C and says that severe hypothermia may require active internal rewarming; consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [N1-F1]. The NIH update similarly says that hypothermic patients with risk factors for imminent cardiac arrest should be transferred directly to an ECLS center, and continuous CPR should be performed if the patient arrests [N5-F2]. The 2021 NIH update also says that rewarming can be accomplished by passive and active techniques, and most often passive and active external techniques are used, while only internal rewarming is required in refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest [N5-F2]. The UpToDate section on accidental hypothermia in adults defines moderate hypothermia as 28°C–32°C and severe hypothermia as <28°C [N6-F3]. So the patient at 28°C is at the threshold of severe hypothermia and clearly warrants urgent rewarming, especially because the temperature is near the point where internal rewarming becomes the preferred mode [N1-F1][N5-F2][N6-F3].

Role of bradycardia in deciding rewarming intensity
Bradycardia is a major clinical sign that supports a more aggressive rewarming approach. ## Executive summary

For severe hypothermia, the best algorithm is temperature-guided, rhythm-guided, and risk-guided. If the patient has a core temperature below 30°C, active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is usually needed when there is cardiac arrest or when external rewarming is refractory [N1-F1][N5-F2]. If the patient is still perfusing and the temperature is moderate (30°C–34°C), active external rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2]. ## 1) Core temperature thresholds for classification and intervention

The branch reports support a clear temperature-based framework:

- **Mild hypothermia:** >34°C [N1-F1]
- **Moderate hypothermia:** 30°C–34°C [N1-F1]
- **Severe hypothermia:** <30°C [N1-F1]
- **Profound hypothermia:** <24°C or <20°C [N6-F3]

The 2021 NIH update also notes that accidental hypothermia is defined as core temperature below 35°C, with further stages based on temperature and clinical signs [N5-F2]. The 2020 Wilderness Medical Society CPG adds that if the body temperature is below 30°C, only one attempt should be made, and further attempts are indicated once the temperature is above 30°C [N7-R3].

So the core temperature thresholds for intervention are:
- **<30°C:** severe hypothermia; active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2][N7-R3]
- **30°C–34°C:** moderate hypothermia; active external rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2]
- **>34°C:** mild hypothermia; passive rewarming may be sufficient [N1-F1][N1-R2]

The algorithm is not one-size-fits-all. The preferred mode depends on the patient’s core temperature and rhythm:

### A) If the patient is still perfusing and the temperature is moderate (30°C–34°C)
External rewarming is usually the first choice [N1-F1]. The Circulation guideline explicitly states that for patients with a perfusing rhythm and moderate hypothermia, active external rewarming is appropriate [N1-F1]. The NIH update similarly says that most often passive and active external techniques are used, while only internal rewarming is required in refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest [N5-F2]. So:

- **Perfusing rhythm, 30°C–34°C:** prefer active external rewarming [N1-F1][N5-F2]

### B) If the patient is in cardiac arrest
Active internal rewarming is needed [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The Circulation guideline says that for patients with a core body temperature <30°C and cardiac arrest, active internal rewarming techniques are needed [N1-R1]. The NIH update similarly says that if a hypothermic patient arrests, continuous CPR should be performed and internal rewarming should be considered, especially if continuous or mechanical CPR is not possible [N5-F2]. So:

- **Cardiac arrest:** active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is needed [N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-F2]

### C) If the patient is at risk for imminent cardiac arrest
The NIH update says that hypothermic patients with risk factors for imminent cardiac arrest should be transferred directly to an ECLS center [N5-F2]. That is an important exception to the usual external-rewarming-first approach.

### D) If the patient is refractory to external rewarming
Internal rewarming becomes required [N5-F2]. The NIH update says that only in patients with refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest are internal rewarming techniques required [N5-F2]. So:

- **Refractory hypothermia:** internal rewarming is required [N5-F2]

## 3) Contraindications or exceptions to active rewarming

Active rewarming is not contraindicated in most hypothermic patients, but it is not the first choice when the patient is in cardiac arrest or when external rewarming is refractory [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### Key exceptions:
- **Cardiac arrest:** active internal rewarming is needed rather than continuing only external rewarming [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Refractory hypothermia:** internal rewarming is required [N5-F2]
- **Temperature <30°C:** only one attempt should be made, and further attempts are indicated once the temperature is above 30°C [N7-R3]

If the patient is extremely cold and has a perfusing rhythm, the goal is not to delay rewarming. The Circulation guideline says rewarming should start prehospital, and for patients with a perfusing rhythm and moderate hypothermia, active external rewarming is appropriate [N1-F1]. So the exception is not a rule against active rewarming; it is a rule for escalating rewarming when the patient is in cardiac arrest or becomes refractory [N1-F1][N5-F2].

## 4) Algorithmic decision points for active external vs active internal rewarming

The evidence supports a staged algorithm rather than a single blunt cutoff. The strongest decision points are temperature and rhythm [N1-F1][N5-F2].

### Key clinical signs that favor external rewarming over internal rewarming
External rewarming is preferred when:
- the patient is perfusing,

So bradycardia in hypothermia is not a reason to avoid rewarming; rather, it is a sign that the patient is likely to benefit from active rewarming, especially internal rewarming if needed.

The main pitfalls in rapid decision-making include:
- delaying rewarming because the patient is bradycardic,
- using pacing or vasopressors without first rewarming,
- assuming external rewarming is sufficient when the patient is near or below 30°C,
- ignoring the need for internal rewarming in cardiac arrest or refractory hypothermia [N1-F1][N4-R3][N5-F2]

- consider internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming if the patient is in cardiac arrest or becomes refractory,
- avoid pacing or rapid heart rate support without first addressing the underlying rewarming need [N1-F1][N5-F2][N4-R3]

## 7) Practical conclusion: a clear reference algorithm

### Step 1: Measure core temperature
- If <30°C, severe hypothermia; active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2]
- If 30°C–34°C, moderate hypothermia; active external rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2]

### Step 4: Monitor continuously

For a patient at 28°C with severe bradycardia, the best algorithm is:

2. **Measure core temperature.**
3. **Start active rewarming.**
4. **Prefer external rewarming if the patient is perfusing and not in cardiac arrest [N1-F1][N5-F2].**
5. **Use internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming if the patient is in cardiac arrest or becomes refractory [N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-F2].**

For severe hypothermia, the best algorithm is temperature-guided, rhythm-guided, and risk-guided. ## 1) Core temperature thresholds for classification and intervention

The branch reports support a clear temperature-based framework:

- **Mild hypothermia:** >34°C [N1-F1]
- **Moderate hypothermia:** 30°C–34°C [N1-F1]
- **Severe hypothermia:** <30°C [N1-F1]
- **Profound hypothermia:** <24°C or <20°C [N6-F3]

The 2021 NIH update also notes that accidental hypothermia is defined as core temperature below 35°C, with further stages based on temperature and clinical signs [N5-F2]. The 2020 Wilderness Medical Society CPG adds that if the body temperature is below 30°C, only one attempt should be made, and further attempts are indicated once the temperature is above 30°C [N7-R3].

So the core temperature thresholds for intervention are:
- **<30°C:** severe hypothermia; active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2][N7-R3]
- **30°C–34°C:** moderate hypothermia; active external rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2]
- **>34°C:** mild hypothermia; passive rewarming may be sufficient [N1-F1][N1-R2]

## 2) When to initiate rewarming and which rewarming mode is preferred

The algorithm is not one-size-fits-all. The preferred mode depends on the patient’s core temperature and rhythm:

### A) If the patient is still perfusing and the temperature is moderate (30°C–34°C)
External rewarming is usually the first choice [N1-F1]. The Circulation guideline explicitly states that for patients with a perfusing rhythm and moderate hypothermia, active external rewarming is appropriate [N1-F1]. The NIH update similarly says that most often passive and active external techniques are used, while only internal rewarming is required in refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest [N5-F2]. So:

- **Perfusing rhythm, 30°C–34°C:** prefer active external rewarming [N1-F1][N5-F2]

### B) If the patient is in cardiac arrest
Active internal rewarming is needed [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The Circulation guideline says that for patients with a core body temperature <30°C and cardiac arrest, active internal rewarming techniques are needed [N1-R1]. The NIH update similarly says that if a hypothermic patient arrests, continuous CPR should be performed and internal rewarming should be considered, especially if continuous or mechanical CPR is not possible [N5-F2]. So:

- **Cardiac arrest:** active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is needed [N1-R1][N1-F1][N5-F2]

### C) If the patient is at risk for imminent cardiac arrest
The NIH update says that hypothermic patients with risk factors for imminent cardiac arrest should be transferred directly to an ECLS center [N5-F2]. That is an important exception to the usual external-rewarming-first approach.

### D) If the patient is refractory to external rewarming
Internal rewarming becomes required [N5-F2]. The NIH update says that only in patients with refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest are internal rewarming techniques required [N5-F2]. So:

- **Refractory hypothermia:** internal rewarming is required [N5-F2]

## 3) Contraindications or exceptions to active rewarming

Active rewarming is not contraindicated in most hypothermic patients, but it is not the first choice when the patient is in cardiac arrest or when external rewarming is refractory [N1-F1][N5-F2].

- **Cardiac arrest:** active internal rewarming is needed rather than continuing only external rewarming [N1-R1][N1-F1]
- **Refractory hypothermia:** internal rewarming is required [N5-F2]
- **Temperature <30°C:** only one attempt should be made, and further attempts are indicated once the temperature is above 30°C [N7-R3]

If the patient is extremely cold and has a perfusing rhythm, the goal is not to delay rewarming. - rewarming is not producing sufficient core temperature increase,

- protecting the patient from further heat loss,
- intubation and vascular access when needed,
- gentle handling to avoid arrhythmias [N1-F1][N5-F2]

- ECG,
- hemodynamic parameters,
- signs of arrhythmia,
- evidence of tissue injury from external rewarming,
- rewarming rate and response [N1-F1][N4-R3][N5-F2]

The rewarming modality or intensity should be switched or paused when:
- the patient becomes unstable,
- external rewarming is not sufficient,
- or hemodynamic instability develops [N1-F1][N5-F2]

The 2020 Wilderness Medical Society CPG adds that if the body temperature is below 30°C, only one attempt should be made, and further attempts are indicated once the temperature is greater than 30°C [N7-R3]. That is a useful threshold for deciding whether to continue external rewarming.

The main pitfalls in rapid decision-making include:
- delaying rewarming because the patient is bradycardic,
- using pacing or vasopressors without first rewarming,
- assuming external rewarming is sufficient when the patient is near or below 30°C,

- avoid pacing or rapid heart rate support without first addressing the underlying rewarming need [N1-F1][N5-F2][N4-R3]

### Step 1: Measure core temperature
- If <30°C, severe hypothermia; active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2]
- If 30°C–34°C, moderate hypothermia; active external rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2]

### Step 3: Escalate if needed
- If the patient remains hemodynamically unstable or rewarming is not sufficient, escalate to internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming [N1-F1][N5-F2]

2. **Measure core temperature.**
3. **Start active rewarming.**
4. **Prefer external rewarming if the patient is perfusing and not in cardiac arrest [N1-F1][N5-F2].**

## Executive summary

For severe hypothermia, the best algorithm is temperature-guided, rhythm-guided, and risk-guided. If the patient has a core temperature below 30°C, active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is usually needed when there is cardiac arrest or when external rewarming is refractory [N1-F1][N5-F2]. ## 1) Core temperature thresholds for classification and intervention

The branch reports support a clear temperature-based framework:

- **Mild hypothermia:** >34°C [N1-F1]
- **Moderate hypothermia:** 30°C–34°C [N1-F1]
- **Severe hypothermia:** <30°C [N1-F1]
- **Profound hypothermia:** <24°C or <20°C [N6-F3]

The 2021 NIH update also notes that accidental hypothermia is defined as core temperature below 35°C, with further stages based on temperature and clinical signs [N5-F2]. The 2020 Wilderness Medical Society CPG adds that if the body temperature is below 30°C, only one attempt should be made, and further attempts are indicated once the temperature is above 30°C [N7-R3].

So the core temperature thresholds for intervention are:
- **<30°C:** severe hypothermia; active internal rewarming or extracorporeal rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2][N7-R3]
- **30°C–34°C:** moderate hypothermia; active external rewarming is usually preferred [N1-F1][N5-F2]
- **>34°C:** mild hypothermia; passive rewarming may be sufficient [N1-F1][N1-R2]

The algorithm is not one-size-fits-all. The preferred mode depends on the patient’s core temperature and rhythm:

### A) If the patient is still perfusing and the temperature is moderate (30°C–34°C)
External rewarming is usually the first choice [N1-F1]. The Circulation guideline explicitly states that for patients with a perfusing rhythm and moderate hypothermia, active external rewarming is appropriate [N1-F1]. The NIH update similarly says that most often passive and active external techniques are used, while only internal rewarming is required in refractory hypothermia or cardiac arrest [N5-F2]. So:
